extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of Chinese literature; writers interested in historical production contexts
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of modern and contemporary Chinese literary movements, norms, censorship practices, and publishing/online-production models from the Republican era through the present. Useful for readers studying how political, social, and market forces shaped literary form and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insistence on socialist realism (Great Leap Forward)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of the Great Leap Forward (1957–59), the government increased its insistence on the use of socialist realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class struggle became a frequent narrative structure and political mode of expression in late-1950s literature. Works from this period used socialist-realist modes to portray social problems and solutions in politically sanctioned terms (examples cited include A Chronicle of Creation and Three Mile Bay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class struggle as narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Class struggle was a frequent narrative structure and political mode of expression in literature of the late 1950s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These narratives depicted class struggle as a way to resolve social conflict, usually through the protagonists uncovering a conspiracy between new and old class enemies; this framing shaped plot choices, character roles (revolutionary vs. reactionary), and thematic binary oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yan'an Talks principles for cultural production (dogmatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles for cultural production laid out by Mao in the 1942 Talks at the Yan'an Forum became dogmatized during the Cultural Revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mao's 1942 directives provided prescriptive aims for literature and art (serving politics and the masses); during the Cultural Revolution those principles hardened into strict controls on acceptable themes, forms, and political orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three prominences principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied in the literary context, the principle of the three prominences was that texts should demonstrate the struggle between revolutionary and reactionary forces in a stark and dichotomous manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aesthetic guideline demanded clear valorization of revolutionary forces and marginalization/condemnation of reactionary forces; it affected characterization, plot emphasis, and rhetorical choices in model works and adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved stage and model works during Cultural Revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), the only stage productions allowed were Jiang Qing's 'Eight Model Operas', while politically orthodox films and heroic novels received official promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic production was restricted to politically approved forms that combined traditional and western forms in service of propaganda; nonconforming theatrical works were effectively banned from official stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre emphasis: long-form novel and sent-down youth narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Cultural Revolution, the long-form novel was an emphasized form of literature; among major genres were novels about the experiences of sent-down youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-favored genres included sustained narrative forms that could convey revolutionary pedagogy or model biographies; works authored by sent-down youths themselves were among notable examples (e.g., Zhang Kangkang's Dividing Line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of art for social campaigns (e.g., birth planning propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local government bureaus and work units composed cultural works such as songs and dramas in an effort to overturn traditional cultural preferences for early marriage, large families, and sons over daughters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural production was used instrumentally to address policy aims; materials (songs, short plays, skits) were created to foreground official messages. Although modern audiences may find such propaganda trite, contemporaneous scholars note these themes spoke directly to widespread social concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scar literature and reportage as truth-claiming genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Scar literature and reportage literature in the early 1980s presented graphic narratives of violence in the Cultural Revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These genres aimed to document and criticize abuses of power, were often patriotic yet cynical about leadership, and influenced related film movements (e.g., Fifth Generation). Their evaluative criterion was often factual-seeming graphicness and moral witness to past abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misty poetry / subjective realism (aesthetic alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four 'misty poets' expressed themselves in deliberately obscure verse which reflected subjective realism rather than the realism of the sort promoted during the Cultural Revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscurity, personal subjectivity, and indirect language were aesthetic markers distinguishing this movement from state-promoted realist clarity; diction and evasive imagery were deliberate stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary experimentation (late 1980s)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second half of the 1980s, writers experimented with modernist language and narrative modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation included formal innovation, unconventional styles, and treatment of sensitive subject matter—examples include Wang Meng, Zhang Xinxin, Gao Xingjian—marking an evaluative shift toward formal daring and inward focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Xungen movement: reconnecting to Chinese traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Xungen movement sought to reconnect literature and culture to Chinese traditions, from which modernization and cultural and political iconoclasm had severed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works in this current emphasized roots, regional cultures, and traditional forms as sources for contemporary literary renewal; evaluative preference favored authentic engagement with local/traditional cultural materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑1989 commercialization of culture and market-driven content
rubrics_metrics.description: After Deng Xiaoping's 1992 southern tour, the culture industry of China became increasingly commercialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercialization produced market-driven genres and writers (e.g., Wang Shuo), and shifted some evaluative standards toward salesability, bestseller potential, and entertainment value alongside—or in tension with—serious literary intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and production norms of Chinese online literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese online literature encompasses works created and consumed on digital platforms, thriving on serialized publication and scrolling-based platforms; platforms like Qidian introduced freemium models and commercialized serialized storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production criteria include: serialized/episodic structure, frequent/consistent updates, responsiveness to reader comments/ratings/gifts, output metrics tied to pay (royalties or salaries), and fandom-driven story steering; successful online authors may optimize for reader engagement, update cadence, and adaptation potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and internationalization practices (online literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms such as Qidian and Jinjiang Literature City cater to market demands, focus on popular genres (fantasy, cultivation), offer flexible contracts, and have enabled authors to earn livelihoods; international platforms and translation teams have brought Chinese genres abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators aiming for commercial success should align with platform genre expectations, consider freemium/monetization strategies, and account for translation/adaptation pathways (including machine-aided translation), while being mindful of ethical/artistic debates around automated translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and publishing regulation (GAPP authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: China's state-run General Administration of Press and Publication (GAPP) screens all Chinese literature intended to be sold on the open market and has the legal authority to screen, censor, and ban any print, electronic, or Internet publication in China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All publishers must be licensed by GAPP; the agency can deny publication rights and shut down publishers who fail to follow directives. Consequences include book burnings, required rewrites (e.g., removal of supernatural references), and a robust underground/bootleg publishing sector where unlicensed works circulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content alteration for regulatory compliance (publication edits/adaptations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works have been rewritten to remove content objectionable to censors before being published in print (example: Ghost Blows Out the Light had to be rewritten to remove references to the supernatural).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and publishers seeking print release may need to preemptively alter themes, scenes, or references that trigger censorship (supernatural, politically sensitive content); this is a pragmatic production constraint shaping narrative choices and genre viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of translation in shaping writers and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Translated literature has long played an important role in modern China; some influential writers were literary translators themselves, and government programs have sponsored translations of approved Chinese works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation functions both as a source of inspiration for writers and as a state-supported channel for international dissemination; evaluative considerations for translated works include selection for cultural diplomacy and alignment with approved themes.
